paras: The attempted lynching of Jeff D. Gillenwaters took place on the night of September 9-10, 1881, when a masked mob took him from the jail at Senatobia, Tate County, Mississippi, where he was held on a charge of murder, and shot him several times outside town. First reports said he would not live, but he survived, named his attackers, and six men were arrested and held without bail. Papers noted the case chiefly because the intended victim lived to identify the lynchers.

Gillenwaters was charged with killing S. T. Eason, a popular young storekeeper of Arkabutla, who was found with his throat cut in the back room of his store, where the two men had often slept as friends. According to the Memphis Appeal's Senatobia correspondent, a bloody shirt, visiting cards and studs identified as his were found in the room, and a magistrate committed him without bail. Many had talked of lynching him, though a Memphis wire called the evidence "only circumstantial."

The raid came about 10 o'clock Friday night by the first special, or about 1 a.m. Saturday by the Appeal and the Panola Star. In the correspondent's account, armed and masked men broke down the jail's back door with a sledge hammer, and the jailer's wife gave up the keys to save her husband's life.

The mob led Gillenwaters west with a rope around his neck, and both the Appeal and the Panola Star said it meant to hang him. When the courthouse bell rang, two deputy sheriffs, the town marshal and others set out after the raiders. About a mile and a half from town the mob shot him, then fled, and the pursuers found him at the gate of a cabin by the road. Accounts of his wounds varied from seven balls to nine shots, and the Public Ledger added that one of the mob clubbed him with a pistol.
Carried to the house of his uncle, D. J. Sherrod, he made a statement naming seven of his attackers while physicians despaired of his life.

By daylight a posse was on the road, and before night six of the seven men he named were in jail. Reports described them as young men from Arkabutla, and the Public Ledger called them "nothing but boys"; a Vicksburg report said fourteen others in the mob had not been arrested. On September 26 Judge Powell heard a habeas corpus petition from Louis P. Sayre, Abe Newton and others and refused bail because physicians could not say Gillenwaters was out of danger.

The six were held without bond, with Gen. J. R. Chalmers retained for their defense. By October 21 the Public Ledger reported that Gillenwaters, well on the way to recovery, had escaped custody, and it hinted that friends of the murdered man had connived in his escape. No report of a trial of either Gillenwaters or the accused lynchers appears in the coverage.

The story first ran as a Senatobia special in the Memphis Public Ledger and spread to Chicago, Savannah, Knoxville, Lancaster and a German-language Baltimore paper, some printing his name as "J. W. Fuller Waters." Several Ohio weeklies said he had been "fatally shot" well after other papers reported him recovering. A second Memphis wire, headlined "Lynchers Who Made a Mistake" in Dallas, stressed the weak evidence and his survival, and later ran in Ohio and Georgia.

Mississippi and Memphis papers divided sharply over the mob. The Public Ledger called Gillenwaters "undoubtedly guilty" of an atrocious murder and remarked that his recognizing the lynchers "perhaps makes no great difference with them." The Panola Star, by contrast, ran a "Lynch Law" editorial demanding "strict and stern justice" for the "masked nightriders," which a Louisiana weekly reprinted. The Appeal's correspondent, under the headline "Mob Law," said good citizens deplored the attempt.
Farther away the case became a filler item that "some lynchers are in trouble," and the Washington Evening Critic joked that the survivor was "amusing himself by identifying all his assailants."

Reports differ on his first name, the hour of the raid, how the mob got the keys, the number of wounds, and whether he walked back to town or was found by the deputies. The Appeal's local letter, written two days after the raid by a Senatobia correspondent, gives the most detailed account of these points.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Jeff D. Gillenwaters
bases: A masked mob took an accused murderer from the Senatobia jail, led him off with a rope around his neck and shot him repeatedly, leaving him for dead (A7, A16); he survived, so the episode is an attempted lynching (A8, A21, A26).

A mob of twenty or thirty took Gillenwaters from jail over his alleged murder of Eason and shot him (A16, A7), but he was alive on Sept. 12 and Sept. 27 and later escaped custody (A8, A21, A26); with no death it is an attempted lynching, not a lynching.

The Senatobia special (A1), the Appeal's local correspondent (A7), a separate Memphis wire (A10) and the Panola Star (A16) independently agree that a masked mob took him from the jail and shot him and that he survived and identified his attackers.

accounts.label: Senatobia special to the Memphis Public Ledger
accounts.gist: A masked mob took J. W. Gillenwaters from jail about 10 p.m. and shot him; he was not expected to live.

accounts.label: Appeal correspondent 'Dark Orange'
accounts.gist: Masked raiders broke into the jail about 1 a.m., got the keys from the jailer's wife, led him off with a rope, and fled after shooting him when the town was roused; deputies found him at a cabin gate and he named seven attackers.

accounts.label: Memphis wire of Sept. 12
accounts.gist: A young mob forced the jailer to open the doors and shot Gillenwaters out of town; the evidence against him was only circumstantial; he regained strength, returned to town and identified six.

accounts.label: Panola Star editorial
accounts.gist: Twenty or thirty men from Arkabutla, intending to hang him, fired seven balls into him and fled when Senatobia citizens raised a rescuing party.

framing.detail: The Memphis Public Ledger called him 'undoubtedly guilty' of 'a most atrocious murder' and said his recognizing the mob 'perhaps makes no great difference with them'.
The Panola Star's 'Lynch Law' editorial demanded 'strict and stern justice' for the 'masked nightriders' whatever the charge against their victim.
The Appeal's correspondent headlined 'Mob Law' and said good citizens deplored the 'mobocracy' that cheated the law.
The Memphis wire headlined 'Lynchers Who Made a Mistake' and stressed the circumstantial evidence.
Northern and western briefs ran it as 'lynchers in trouble' or, in the Washington Evening Critic, as a joke that 'turn about is fair play'.
